results.topic: Oppenheimer's use of practical effects and IMAX filmmaking

result.text: Watching Oppenheimer in 70mm IMAX proves that digital effects will never replicate the terrifying weight of practical filmmaking. Nolan turned an intimate historical drama into a visceral, bone-rattling masterpiece through sheer technical craft and the raw power of celluloid.

results.topic: Whether streaming has killed the theatrical experience

result.text: Streaming didn’t kill the theatrical experience—it exposed how lazy studios became. You can’t replicate the communal magic of a dark room and a massive screen on a couch. Cinema isn’t dead; it just raised the bar for what’s actually worth leaving the house for.

results.topic: The Brutalist and its 3.5 hour runtime

result.text: Don’t let the 3.5-hour runtime scare you away—The Brutalist earns every single minute of its monumental length. Brady Corbet has crafted a staggering, uncompromising epic that makes modern two-hour movies feel bloated by comparison.

Superhero fatigue isn’t about being tired of capes; it’s about being exhausted by homework. When every movie feels like a two-hour commercial for the next project rather than a self-contained story with real stakes and distinct vision, audiences naturally check out.

Dune: Part Two’s desert cinematography is an absolute masterclass in scale and texture. Greig Fraser captures Arrakis with a brutal, sun-bleached majesty that makes the sand feel tangible and the world overwhelmingly real. Cinema was made for visuals like this.

results.topic: The Oscar nominations being predictable this year

result.text: Watching this year’s Oscar nominations felt less like celebrating the best in cinema and more like reading a pre-approved corporate memo, as the Academy once again refused to embrace a single genuine surprise.
